domains.note: No search (databases, terms, dates) and no selection process is reported anywhere in the paper. The only stated criterion is that studies with HIV-positive participants were excluded (p. 592), and the studies in Tables 1-4 (pp. 590-604) are listed without saying how they were found or chosen.

Every study in Tables 1-4 gets a 'Caveats' column (education mismatch, other drug use, small samples, no comparison with norms) and the text critiques studies one by one (pp. 596-602). But no appraisal method is stated, the authors' own comparisons of McCann 2008 and Simon 2002 with published norms give neither the norms nor the values (pp. 596, 602), and non-significant results from small samples are coded as users and controls having 'performed equally' (table keys, pp. 595, 601, 604).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Hart is an author on 8 of the 88 references (none name Marvin, Silver or Smith), but these are 7 of the 16 acute-dosing studies in Table 1 (pp. 590-591), including Hart et al. 2008, the main high-dose intranasal study in dependent users behind the abstract's claim that methamphetamine acutely improves cognition (p. 592). The long-term sections (Tables 2-4) rest on other groups' studies.

The abstract says users' cognition 'overwhelmingly falls within the normal range when compared against normative data' (p. 586), yet Tables 2-4 mark most studies as never compared with norms, so their clinical importance 'could not be determined'. The conclusions then call the impairment link 'not supported by evidence from research' and treatment concerns 'not warranted' (p. 605), which the body never tested; only the closing comparison with crack cocaine is labelled as speculation.

Balance of evidence for and against cognitive impairment in methamphetamine users: the evidence for impairment is under-represented. The one meta-analysis (Scott et al. 2007) is mentioned only as 'the dominant view', with none of its results (p. 587), and the one study classifying individual users against norms (Kalechstein 2003, about twice as many users as controls impaired) is set aside as possibly distorted by its small sample (p. 602).

sc_hart_2012.reasoning: No search or selection method is reported, and the summary claims (cognition 'overwhelmingly' within the normal range; the impairment link 'not supported by evidence') go beyond a body in which most studies were never compared with norms. The per-study caveat tables and the distinction between a statistical difference and a clinical dysfunction are real strengths, but the meta-analytic evidence for impairment is not engaged and much of the acute-dosing evidence comes from the authors' own laboratory. Three domains are high, so the overall is high.

domains.note: No search (databases, terms, dates) or screening process is reported. Explicit eligibility criteria are given only for the matched cross-sectional studies (p. 261), so the selection behind the other five lines of evidence, and statements such as 'only one study' of twins (p. 263) or 'only two longitudinal studies' (p. 264), cannot be checked.

Designs are appraised throughout: Table 1 records matching and unmatched confounds (pp. 262-263), and the text flags practice effects in retest studies without controls (pp. 263-265) and the twin study's lack of urine testing (p. 263). But no method is stated and the scrutiny is uneven: two null studies are discounted because Bonferroni correction 'may be overly conservative' (p. 261), while brain studies of 5-12 users are called 'convincing' (p. 265), including the authors' own Figure 1, shown at an uncorrected threshold (p. 266).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 10 of the 129 references come from the authors' group (9 list Dean, Groman, Morales or London as authors; Berman 2007 is described as from 'the same laboratory', p. 265), a small share. But they carry specific steps of the argument: the only primate escalating-dose study (Groman 2012, pp. 260-261), two of the five longitudinal brain studies plus Figure 1 (Berman 2007, Morales 2012, pp. 265-266), and the education argument with Figure 2 (Dean 2012, pp. 267-268).

The abstract's hedged conclusion ('mixed', 'possibility', 'at least some users', p. 259) matches the body, and the moderators section is framed as hypothesis. But a post-hoc trend in Iudicello 2010 (p = 0.06, subgroups as small as n = 6, p. 264) becomes a finding that a subset improves with abstinence (pp. 264, 269), and brain changes during abstinence are counted among 'five of our six' supported hypotheses although the body says their link to cognition is unclear (pp. 265, 269).

Balance of evidence for and against a causal effect of methamphetamine on cognition: null cross-sectional studies, the mostly null dose-response studies, animal studies in which escalating doses prevented deficits, and Hart et al.'s critique are all presented and answered (pp. 260-270), so neither side is clearly under-represented. Minor tilts are the discounting of Bonferroni-corrected nulls (p. 261) and the passing, parenthetical treatment of the Ersche 2012 sibling study (p. 263).

sc_dean_2013.reasoning: A carefully structured review that tests six stated hypotheses, reports null and contrary findings and reaches a hedged conclusion. With no reported search and explicit criteria for only one of its six lines of evidence, however, its 'preponderance' judgment cannot be checked for completeness, which makes the selection domain, and so the overall, high. Some summary statements overstate weak findings, and the authors' own studies carry the primate, longitudinal-imaging and education steps.

domains.note: The end of the Introduction reports a search of PubMed and national survey databases in April 2014 (repeated September 2014), with example terms ('methamphetamine', 'psychosis' and domain terms 'such as' epidemiology or treatment). No inclusion criteria or selection process are given beyond an effort to include 'the most recent reports and reviews'.

Most studies are reported as findings without their design, sample or limitations, for example the 'up to 40%' prevalence (Section 2), the fivefold familial risk (3.1), the Thai cohort's nearly 40% conversion to schizophrenia (3.2) and the Matrix Model's 'strong evidence of efficacy' (5.2). Appraisal is limited to occasional remarks, such as the single small trial in the Cochrane review (5.1) and the diagnostic interviews' reliance on self-report (Section 4), with no stated method.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 4 of the 99 references carry Glasner-Edwards or Mooney as authors (refs 10, 11, 87, 96), a small share. But ref 10 alone supports the claim that psychotic users engage in Matrix Model treatment and reduce use as much as others (Section 2.1), and the Matrix Model's 'strong evidence of efficacy' (Section 5.2) rests on work by Rawson (refs 91-93), co-author of three of the four self-cited papers.

The abstract states that psychosocial treatment 'has a strong evidence base and is the optimal first-line treatment approach to reducing rates of psychosis', whereas Section 2.1 says only that this 'has been argued' (without a citation) and Section 5.2 notes that CBT 'has not been formally studied' for methamphetamine-induced psychosis. Elsewhere speculation is mostly marked with 'may'.

Balance of evidence on the course and treatment of methamphetamine psychosis: competing explanations of persistent psychosis (Section 3.2) and both the benefits and the risks of antipsychotics (Section 5.1) are presented. Psychosocial treatment, however, appears only favourably, with no effect sizes, relapse rates or limitations (Sections 5.2-5.3), so the evidence limiting its efficacy is under-represented.

sc_glasner_edwards_2014.reasoning: A clinically oriented review whose brief PubMed search comes without inclusion criteria or a selection account, and which reports most studies without appraising their designs; these two high domains make the overall high. Its headline treatment message is stated more firmly in the abstract than in the body and leans on studies by the authors and their senior co-author. It is useful for its diagnostic framework and as a source of pointers.

domains.note: The 'Inclusion criteria' and 'Search approach' sections give explicit a-priori criteria, three databases plus Google Scholar and reference lists, and the full search string. Search dates and any account of screening (numbers found, excluded, included) are missing, and one included study (ref 117) appears in Table 2 and the text but not in Table 1.

Table 2 appraises each included study on fixed points (comparison groups, acute versus chronic, abstinence, confounds), and 'Methodological limitations and considerations' covers power, other drug use, medication and rating scales. But some studies are misreported or labelled inconsistently: the text says ref 109 found more visual and tactile hallucinations in transient than in persistent or primary psychosis, whereas Table 1 reports the opposite direction, and ref 116 is 'Chronic MAP' in Table 1 but 'assumed ... acute' in Table 2.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 140 references has Wearne or Cornish as an author, so none of the evidence comes from the authors' own studies.

The abstract presents thought disorder, visual and tactile hallucinations and parietal-linked attention deficits as features by which acute METH psychosis 'could be clinically distinguished', but the body calls the thought-disorder and hallucination evidence 'indirect and inconclusive' and not 'reliable' (Positive symptoms), and the parietal link is the authors' inference from one small study (ref 106, Cognitive symptoms). The treatment ideas are clearly labelled 'not clinical recommendations' (Summary and conclusions).

Balance of evidence for similarity versus difference between METH psychosis and schizophrenia: direct comparisons finding no difference (e.g., refs 107, 108, 110, 111, 116) are reported alongside those finding differences (refs 112-115), and the Summary and conclusions state both, so neither side is under-represented in the body. The tilt toward difference lies in the abstract and is recorded under evidence versus speculation.

sc_wearne_2018.reasoning: It reports a search, explicit inclusion criteria and a per-study methodological table, and cites none of its authors' own work, so its selection is largely reproducible. Search dates and the screening process are missing, some included studies are misreported or inconsistently classified, and the abstract offers as distinguishing features findings that the body calls indirect or inconclusive. No domain is high, so the overall is some concerns.

domains.note: No search, inclusion criteria or selection process is reported. The abstract says the review 'summarizes the findings' of imaging studies, and the text moves straight into topic sections.

Most studies are reported as findings without their design, sample size or limitations, and no appraisal method is stated. Caveats appear only occasionally (smoking and premorbid differences in Structural Brain Imaging; Boileau 2012's polydrug sample and Chou 2007's five participants in Monoamine systems), and the group's own Figure 1 is shown at an uncorrected threshold without comment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The bibliography mostly shows only first authors: 6 of 142 entries name a review author (London 2004, Payer 2011, Kohno 2013 and 2014, Morales 2012, Ballard 2014), and at least 7 more are London-group papers according to the Hart and Dean reference lists or this text (Berman 2008a and 2008b, Lee 2009, Monterosso 2005 and 2007, Simon 2010, Dean 2012). The group's studies supply Figures 1, 3 and 4, the whole resting-state section (Kohno 2014) and a good part of the decision-making and Implications for Therapy sections.

The abstract's descriptive summary matches the body and the therapy ideas are hedged ('may be considered', 'preliminary'). But the body moves from cross-sectional group differences to causal wording ('consistent with drug-induced white-matter damage' in Structural Brain Imaging; 'methamphetamine-induced inflammation and neurodegeneration are likely behaviorally relevant' in Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation), and the anti-inflammatory and exercise proposals rest on a mouse study and a conference abstract (Implications for Therapy).

Balance of evidence on whether the imaging differences reflect dysfunction caused by methamphetamine: premorbid and smoking explanations (Ersche 2012, Morales 2012) and a few null findings are noted (Structural Brain Imaging; Monoamine systems). But the argument that such differences are often small, unreplicated or unlinked to impaired cognition is not engaged (Hart et al. 2012 is not cited), so the evidence against a dysfunction reading is under-represented.

sc_london_2015.reasoning: A lab-centred overview with no reported search or selection and little appraisal of the cited studies; those two high domains make the overall high. The authors' group supplies three of the four figures and the connectivity and decision-making evidence, and the text at times reads cross-sectional differences as drug-caused damage. It is useful as a map of imaging findings and pointers, not as evidence that methamphetamine causes the abnormalities.
